title: Your Immune System Ages in Two Big Bursts - Nautilus
gist: Duke University-led immunologists analysed gene activity in 3.8 million immune cells from nearly 2,000 healthy Singaporeans aged 19-97, finding that the immune system ages in two big bursts of remodeling in the 40s and 60s (per the article's framing).

insights.claim: Immune system aging appears to happen in two big bursts, with a person's 40s and 60s being periods of intense remodeling rather than a steady decline.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Non-linear immune aging suggests specific age windows for vaccination, screening or intervention, relevant to healthcare and longevity markets.
insights.quote: Your 40s and 60s are periods of intense remodeling
insights.locator: Your Immune System Ages in Two Big Bursts

insights.claim: The most dramatic age-related bodily changes may be invisible ones, such as immune system remodeling, rather than visible ones like wrinkles, weight gain or muscle loss.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shifts attention of aging research toward internal biomarkers over cosmetic markers.
insights.quote: the most dramatic alterations may be happening beneath the surface
insights.locator: Obviously our bodies change a lot

insights.claim: Researchers led by Duke University immunologists examined the genetic activity of 3.8 million immune cells from close to 2,000 healthy people aged 19 to 97 in Singapore, publishing in Nature Communications.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Large single-cell datasets are enabling age-resolved immune maps, though an Asian single-country cohort may limit generalizability.
insights.quote: They investigated the genetic activity of 3.8 million immune cells from close to 2,000 healthy people between the ages of 19 and 97 in Singapore
